name: Popol Vuh K'iche' Maya narrative tradition
tradition: K'iche' Maya narrative and textual tradition
candidate_type: creation narrative / heroic cycle / transmitted sacred text

discovery.summary: Library of Congress and Metropolitan Museum sources identify the Popol Vuh as a K'iche' Maya text containing creation narrative material and document its surviving transmission history. The Library of Congress describes Francisco Ximénez's early-eighteenth-century K'iche'-Spanish transcription as one of the earliest surviving copies and notes scholarly views that it derives from an earlier sixteenth-century alphabetic version, while the Met documents later artistic reception of the text.
discovery.why_relevant: This candidate adds Mesoamerican coverage and provides an excellent case for MFTL's text-transmission model: oral performance, earlier lost or hypothesized forms, surviving colonial transcription, translation, and modern artistic reception can be stored as distinct provenance layers rather than flattened into one undated 'myth'.

sources.title: Popol Vuh: Transcription in Quiché Mayan and Translation into Spanish - Library of Congress
sources.notes: Library of Congress record supports the K'iche' language context, Francisco Ximénez transcription dated approximately 1700–1715, side-by-side Spanish translation, oral-performance character of the text, and the qualified scholarly view that this surviving copy may derive from an earlier sixteenth-century alphabetic version. Accessed 2026-09-07T13:45:20Z.

sources.title: Portfolio: 'Popol-Vuh' - The Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.notes: Metropolitan Museum record identifies Popol Vuh as a K'iche' Maya sacred text containing a creation account and documents Carlos Mérida's 1943 visual interpretation, useful as evidence for later reception rather than for reconstructing the earliest textual form. Accessed 2026-09-07T13:45:20Z.

notes: Material claim mapping: surviving manuscript/transcription history, language, approximate Ximénez date, oral-performance character, and qualified earlier-version hypothesis -> Library of Congress; classification as K'iche' Maya sacred/creation text and 1943 artistic reception -> Metropolitan Museum. Earlier textual forms should remain explicitly uncertain unless supported by stronger manuscript scholarship. Theological assessment intentionally not performed.
